scenes.name: Joy Division
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: De Warsaw, rock pesado con influencias punk, a la desolación ballardiana: la originalidad crece a medida que las canciones se vuelven lentas y ralas, con el bajo de Peter Hook llevando la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner abriendo huecos, la batería de Stephen Morris rodeando un cráter y Ian Curtis recitando desde «un lugar solitario». Martin Hannett, productor de Factory, convierte el espacio en «control atmosférico» con delays digitales y grabaciones separadas: Unknown Pleasures (1979), con la portada del púlsar de Peter Saville, «Transmission», «Atmosphere». El coqueteo con la imaginería nazi, la epilepsia, los barbitúricos y un matrimonio roto desembocan en Closer, «estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtis», y en su suicidio en mayo de 1980. «Love Will Tear Us Apart» es su primer hit. Los supervivientes empiezan de cero como New Order.

podcast.title: Lyrical Shift in Late 1979/1980
podcast.body: Ian Curtis's lyrics composed in late 1979 and 1980 for *Closer* were described as somewhat more "banales" – simpler, less overtly passionate, and less depressing – compared to his earlier work, allowing the band's instrumental contributions to shine through more. "las letras que compuso Ian Cortes a final de 79 y en el 80 que formarían parte de este close up y eran un poco más vanales no eran como tan pasionales ni tan deprimentes a lo mejor son como un peline más sencillas."

podcast.title: Death by Suicide (1980)
podcast.body: Ian Curtis died by his own hand on May 18th, 1980, at the age of 23. His health had been very poor, exacerbated by epileptic seizures, a mix of prescriptions, drinking, illegal drug use, a poor diet, and late nights. He was also under immense pressure from an impending divorce, an affair, financial worries, and the demands of performing with his band, Joy Division. "Ian died by his own hand on May 18th, 1980."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Hours Of...

podcast.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 1980)
podcast.body: Ian Curtis died by suicide on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures exacerbated by a "crazy cocktail" of prescriptions, drinking, illegal drug use, poor diet, and late nights. He also faced an impending divorce, an affair with a Belgian woman, money worries, and pressure to continue performing with Joy Division despite his problems. The final Joy Division show on May 2, 1980, saw Ian faint during the last song, experiencing another grand mal seizure, leading to the cancellation of their upcoming North American tour. On the evening of May 17, Ian returned to his home at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife Deborah was out. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on May 18, he put on his favorite album, "The Idiot" by Iggy Pop, went to the garden for a length of rope from the clothesline, and hanged himself. Deborah found him a few hours later. "He'd been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures that were exacerbated by a crazy cocktail of prescriptions, drinking illegal drug use, poor diet late nights, an impending divorce, and a ferry was having with a woman from Belgium worries about money and pressures to keep on performing with the band despite all these problems."

podcast.body: Ian Curtis's body was found a few hours later by his wife, Deborah. He was 23 years old at the time of his death. "It was Deborah who would find him a few hours later. Ian Curtis, dead by suicide on May 18th, 1980, age 23."

podcast.title: Final Hours and Suicide (1980)
podcast.body: On the evening of May 17th, Ian returned to his house at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife, Deborah, was working as a bartender at a wedding reception. They spoke, and Ian requested time alone, with Deborah agreeing not to return until after 10 AM the next morning, spending the night at her parents' house. After she left, Ian watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank several cups of strong coffee and a shot of whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on Sunday, May 18th, he put on Iggy Pop's "The Idiot," retrieved a rope from his garden's clothesline, and hanged himself. "Once she was gone, Ian sat down to watch his movie, which was a 1977 film entitled Strozek, which follows a musician and form a mental patient who travels to the US and is unable to decide between the two women in his life."

podcast.title: Pre-Suicide Activities (1980)
podcast.body: In the days leading up to his death, Ian seemed to be in good spirits, with no seizures reported. On Thursday, May 15th, 1980, he played pool with bassist Peter Hook. The next day, Peter dropped Ian off at his parents' house with instructions to pack for the upcoming American tour. On Saturday, May 17th, Ian bailed on plans to water ski with guitarist Barney Sumner, citing a need to rest and wanting to watch a cool movie on TV. "On Thursday May 15th, 1980, Ian hung out with bass player Peter Hook playing pool in a local pub."

As the sun came up on May 18, he put on Iggy Pop's album "The Idiot," retrieved a rope from the garden clothesline, and hanged himself. podcast.title: Suicide Details - May 1980
podcast.body: In early May 1980, Ian Curtis, in the midst of divorce proceedings, went to his home, presumably to collect belongings, and finding no one there, got drunk, played Iggy Pop's *The Idiot* album, and tragically hanged himself while alone, with his wife and baby not present. "ancurtis estaba en pleno proceso de divorcio para abandonar a su mujer, va un día a su casa se cree que posiblemente a recoger parte de sus cosas no hay nadie y ancurtis en borracha pone el álbum de idiota de y hip hop y finalmente decida orcarse estando solo en casa mientras su mujer y su bebé no estaban en casa."

podcast.title: "Control" Documentary Reliability
podcast.body: The documentary film "Control," which depicts Ian Curtis's life, is widely regarded as not entirely reliable. This skepticism stems from the fact that his widow was both the producer and the financial backer of the film, which many believe compromised its objectivity. "su productora y la persona que pusó el dinero fue su vida. Entonces tampoco es una versión muy fiable de la que fue la vida de Iain Cortis."

podcast.title: Affair with Annik Honoré
podcast.body: On October 16, 1979, while playing a gig at Plan K in Brussels, Belgium, Ian met Annik Honoré, a woman described as resembling Siouxsie Sioux. This encounter quickly evolved into a full-blown affair, with Ian frequently fabricating excuses to meet Annik, who subsequently moved to London and worked at the Belgian Embassy, and even toured with the band on their European dates in early 1980. "On October 16, 1979, the band played a gig at a place called Plan K in Brussels, Belgium. This is where Ian met a woman named Anik on a ray."

podcast.title: Alignment with Martin Hannett on Closer
podcast.body: During the production of *Closer*, Ian Curtis showed a strong affinity for Martin Hannett's approach and vision, often aligning himself with the producer's creative direction. "Ian Cortes está muy cercano al martin jane."

podcast.title: Allergies and Mood Swings
podcast.body: Ian suffered from health challenges beyond drug-related incidents, including an allergy to sunlight (polyformus-like eruption) that caused his hands to swell like "big red balloons," requiring bandaging. He also exhibited "Jekyll and Hyde mood swings," once throwing a drink at Deborah at their engagement party, and in the band, his erratic behavior was termed "alter Ian," leading to strange actions like kicking in a door or getting into fights. "For example, he was allergic to sunlight. He had something called polyformus-like eruption."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Thom Yorke
podcast.body: Ian Curtis was mentioned in a late 1995 *Melody Maker* article about Thom Yorke, which controversially suggested Yorke might be the "next martyr of rock." The article drew parallels between Yorke, Curtis, and Kurt Cobain, predicting Yorke's "imminent" suicide due to depression. "comparándolo con Ian Curtis"

podcast.title: Conflicting Accounts of Death
podcast.body: Years after Ian Curtis's death, those who were part of his life, including his ex-wife, Martin Hannett, Tony Wilson, and other band members, have offered their own biographies and versions of events, which frequently conflict with each other and even with their own previous accounts over time. "han pasado tantos años que casi todos los que formaron parte de la vida de Ian Courtesy en su día tienen como su propia biografía su propia versión y su propia historia muchas veces no concordan demasiado muchas veces incluso sus propias historias a lo largo de los años no concordan demasiado entonces según leas a lo que iba a ser la es mujer de Ian Courtesy o a Martin Hannet o a Toni Wilson o a los otros miembros en la banda pues la historia cambia bastante."

podcast.title: Dancing as a Symptom
podcast.body: Ian's distinctive "herky-jerky" dancing during live performances of Joy Division was often so erratic that it was difficult to distinguish from an actual epileptic seizure, leading to confusion among audiences and even band members about his true condition. "When joint division played live, Ian would dance in a very herky jirky sort of way, almost as if he was being electrocuted or something. Was he dancing or was he suffering another seizure?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Darkening Lyrics and Poetry
podcast.body: Ian consistently carried a plastic bag filled with notebooks, where he would write poetry and lyrics whenever inspiration struck. As these writings were adapted into Joy Division's music, the band's sound became increasingly somber, dark, and depressing, with nearly all compositions written in a minor key. "And finally, more people began to notice that Ian's lyrics and poetry were becoming darker and more depressing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Day Jobs and Punk Discovery
podcast.body: After finding a house with Deborah (eventually settling at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, where he had a room for his poetry), Ian initially worked in a record store in downtown Manchester, where he discovered punk rock. He later secured more stable employment within the British Civil Service, moving between several parts of the bureaucracy, such as the Ministry of Defense and an unemployment office. "He got a day job in a record store at downtown Manchester, which is where he discovered punk rock."

podcast.body: Ian Curtis, the singer for Joy Division, died in May 1980. His passing led to the remaining members of Joy Division reorganizing themselves into New Order, with the addition of a keyboard player, marking a significant transition in their musical trajectory. "When Joy Division singer Ian Curtis died in May 1980, the band added a keyboard player and reorganized itself into New Order."

podcast.title: Death and Contributing Factors
podcast.body: Born July 15, 1956, and died May 18, 1980, at age 23. He died by suicide, hanging himself in his kitchen after a prolonged battle with depression, which was compounded by manic depression, a worsening case of epilepsy, and a failed romance outside of his marriage. "But after he died, he hung himself in the kitchen after a long bud with depression, exacerbated by manic depression, a worsening case of epilepsy, and a failed romance with a person, not his wife."

podcast.title: Early Life and Influences
podcast.body: Born in Manchester on July 15, 1956, Ian Curtis's father was a police detective, and he had a younger sister named Carol. Raised in Hudsfield, outside Manchester, he sang in the church choir and was an avid reader, delving into Dostoyevsky, Sartre, and other philosophers, as well as literature and poetry, alongside a fascination with military history, particularly Nazi Germany. "Ian was born in Manchester on July 15, 1956. His father was a police detective and he had a younger sister named Carol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Early Marriage and Poetic Preoccupation
podcast.body: On August 23, 1974, Ian married his girlfriend, Deborah, whom he had met when he was 16. Deborah found him mysterious and cool, and was intrigued by a box full of poetry he had written, some of which contained romantic fantasies about him dying young. "But then again, some of that poetry contained romantic fantasies involving Ian dying young."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Epilepsy Diagnosis
podcast.body: After collapsing at a gig as a teenager from strobe lights and learning about epilepsy through his civil service job in 1977, Ian experienced his first confirmed epileptic seizure on December 27, 1978, in the band's van returning from their first London gig. He was hospitalized, and after being on a waiting list, saw a specialist on January 23, 1978 (transcribed year, likely 1979 in context), who prescribed anti-convulsive drugs. "This was Ian's first confirmed epileptic seizure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Evolution of Punk Lyrics
podcast.body: Ian Curtis, through his work with Joy Division, took the punk rock genre and elevated its lyrical content to a previously unexplored sphere. He introduced themes of psychology, intimacy, and profound personal suffering into rock and punk lyrics, transforming the depth of the genre's expression. "Y en Cortis, que con Joy Division, hereda el PANC y lleva las letras, todo este rock PANC, una esfera prácticamente desconocida, en la que se habla, pues, de aspectos de psicología, de intimismo, de sufrimiento personal, que son increíbles."

podcast.title: Expulsion and Substance Abuse
podcast.body: Ian was expelled from school for coming to class high on cough medicine and was also a fan of solvents, Valium, and various barbiturates. With no money to buy records, he regularly stole them from local record stores. "He was also a fan of solvents, volume, and various barbituits. With no money to buy records, he regularly stole them from local record stores."

podcast.title: Final Months Mystery
podcast.body: The period of three to four months that elapsed between the recording of "Love Will Tear Us Apart" and Ian Curtis's tragic suicide is described as particularly interesting, yet there is a scarcity of detailed information regarding this specific timeframe. "los tres, cuatro meses que pasaron entre que grabaron el LoFwiki y el tráfico suicidio de Iain Cortis, en el cual no hay mucha información."

srcs.episode: Love will Tear us appart. Una historia increible.

podcast.title: Formation of the Band
podcast.body: Ian's interest in music intensified after being one of a few dozen people to see the Sex Pistols play the Manchester Free Trade Hall on July 20, 1976, easily identifiable by his jacket with the word "hate" on the back. He then formed a band with Peter Hook and Bernard Albrecht, two guys he kept bumping into again and again at concerts, including that Pistols gig. "His interest in music really took off when he was one of a few dozen people in the audience, when the sex pistols played the Manchester Free Hall on July 20th, 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Gravestone Inscription
podcast.body: The title of "Love Will Tear Us Apart" is famously inscribed on Ian Curtis's gravestone. Although his original gravestone was stolen in 2018 and subsequently replaced, the song title has remained on his memorial marker since the day of his death. "desde el día de su muerte su la pida pone el título de esta canción."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Love will Tear us appart. Una historia increible.

podcast.title: Headstone Inscription
podcast.body: Following the inquest into his death, which officially ruled "Asphyxia with ligature around the neck," Ian Curtis's body was cremated. His wife, Deborah, chose the poignant inscription for his headstone in Macclesfield Cemetery: "Ian Curtis, 18580, Love will Terrorist Apart" (transcribed verbatim from the source). "His body was cremated, and it was Deborah, who selected the inscription for Ian's headstone, laid in Maclisfield Cemetery. It reads, Ian Curtis, 18580, Love will Terrorist Apart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Increased Seizures and Mounting Pressures
podcast.body: As Joy Division's popularity increased, the more gigs they played and the harder they worked, the worse and more frequent Ian's epileptic attacks became, suffering four grand mal seizures in one night in May 1979. By April 1980, the intense pressures from recording the "Closer" album, an ongoing tour, an impending North American tour, his failing marriage, guilt over fatherhood, his demanding mistress, and his continued use of alcohol and drugs exacerbated his epilepsy, making his mood swings unpredictable and leading to a state where he couldn't fall asleep until he had a seizure. "It got to the point where he couldn't fall asleep until he had a seizure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Lyrics Reflecting Decline
podcast.body: Looking back at Ian Curtis's lyrics, it is easy to trace his "slide into crushing depression," reflecting his genuine mental illness. "looking back on Ian's lyrics is now easy to trace his slide into crushing the pressure."

podcast.title: Marriage and Family
podcast.body: Ian Curtis was married to Deborah when he was 19 and she was 18. Four years later, on April 16, 1979, they had a daughter named Natalie. "His wife's name was Deborah. They got married when he was 19 and she was 18 and then four years later on April 16th of 1979 they had Natalie."

podcast.title: Medical Conditions
podcast.body: Ian Curtis was a sickly individual who suffered from two serious medical conditions. He had Porphyria, a rare condition that made him allergic to sunlight, and epilepsy, which caused seizures that became increasingly frequent and severe towards the end of his life. "Ian was a sickly dude who had a rare condition called Porphyria. It caused him to be allergic to sunlight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People

podcast.title: Non-Musician Guitarist
podcast.body: Ian Curtis was not a trained musician and lacked the ability to play instruments. "Love Will Tear Us Apart" is notable as the sole song where he played the guitar, doing so in a "very aggressive" style, using only a few chords. "no sabía tocar instrumentos, se le eran gran triste pero no era músico y en esa canción sí que es la única en la que tomo unos pocos acordes en toda su descordación."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Love will Tear us appart. Una historia increible.

podcast.title: On-Stage Collapse and Overdose Attempt
podcast.body: On April 4, 1980, during a show with The Stranglers at London's Rainbow venue, Ian suffered three epileptic attacks within the first five songs before completely collapsing; the band struggled to intervene earlier due to the difficulty of distinguishing his seizures from his characteristic dancing. Three days later, on April 7, Ian deliberately overdosed on his epilepsy medication, leaving a suicide note, and required a stomach pump at the hospital, yet a psychiatrist controversially declared him "not suicidal." "Three days later, Ian purposely overdosed on his epilepsy medication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Post-Song Life Details
podcast.body: After the publication of "Love Will Tear Us Apart," Ian Curtis lived for an additional three months. During this period, the song began to achieve relative success, and he was reportedly listening to hip-hop at home. His subsequent death left his wife a widow with a small child and forced the cancellation of Joy Division's impending US tour, which was scheduled to commence a week later. "Al estuvo tres meses más en los cuales el disco salió y empezó a terrativo éxito, el sarco, el miembros se escuchaba en su casa en Diadol, de Yipop, su mujer se quedó vio de la comuna niña pequeña."

srcs.episode: Love will Tear us appart. Una historia increible.

podcast.title: Posthumous Financial Success
podcast.body: Although he died poor at age 23, Ian Curtis is now considered "very rich" due to the significant increase in Joy Division's record sales and lasting influence following his death. "Ian Curtis, July 15th, 1956, to May 18th, 1980, died poor at age 23, and now very rich."

podcast.title: Posthumous Legacy
podcast.body: Ian Curtis has become a mythical "doom figure" in Alt Rock following his death. "Now Ian has gone on to become a mythical doom figure in Alt Rock."

podcast.title: Profound Impact on Bono
podcast.body: Bono, the lead singer of U2, was deeply affected by his encounter with Ian Curtis at Strawberry Studios when U2 was an unknown, nascent band. Bono, who was 26 at the time, described Curtis as a tall, thin figure who sang aggressively but, outside of recording, was remarkably articulate and possessed a very good vocabulary. This meeting left a lasting impression on Bono, who has recounted it numerous times in interviews. "le impactó un montón de Ian Cortis que han sido muy alto, muy delgado que cantaba de esa manera tan agresiva pero que sin embargo cuando salía de la grabación en auntía hable, en auntía muy correcto hablando, tenía muy buen vocabulario."

podcast.title: School Dislike and Early Drug Use
podcast.body: Despite his intellectual interests, Ian hated school, preferring to stay home with his books and records by Iggy Pop, The Doors, David Bowie, and Lou Reed rather than attend class. Obligatory visits to local retirement homes with classmates were depressing but also led to rifling through medicine cabinets for medication. "Ian hated school. He would rather stay home with his books and Iggy Pop and Doors and David Bowie and Lou Reed records than go to class."

podcast.title: Significant Health and Personal Struggles
podcast.body: Leading up to his death, Ian Curtis was grappling with substantial health issues and severe personal problems, which were a significant factor in the band's overall turmoil. podcast.title: Suicide by Hanging
podcast.body: After a tumultuous period marked by a collapsing marriage, his mistress's demands, and severe anxiety about the upcoming North American tour, Ian spent the night of May 17, 1980, alone at 77 Barton Street. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, wrote a long note to Deborah with pictures of his wife and baby daughter nearby, then put on Iggy Pop's "The Idiot," and, as the sun rose on Sunday, May 18th, he took a length of rope from the clothesline and hanged himself at the age of 23, discovered by Deborah hours later. "Then he went out into the garden and got himself a length of rope from the clothesline. And as the sun came up and he sang, Ian hanged himself."

podcast.title: Suicide's Impact on Goth Scene
podcast.body: Ian Curtis's suicide contributed to the dark atmosphere and themes prevalent in the developing Goth scene. "And then Ian Curtis of Joy Division committed suicide at adding fuel to that fire."

podcast.title: Tony Wilson's Post-Facto Perspective
podcast.body: In a 2005 interview, Tony Wilson revealed that those close to Ian Curtis, including the band members, knew he was very ill but underestimated the likelihood of suicide, and his death did not entirely surprise them, reflecting a heavy sense of remorse for not having intervened more effectively. "Tony Wilson dijo literalmente sabíamos que Ian Cortes estaba muy mal, sabíamos que no estaba bien, pero subestimamos la posibilidad de que esto pasara y daba a entender además muy clara que ni a la banda ni a él ni a nadie les sorprendió demasiado el que Ian Cortes es suicidada."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis

podcast.title: Tragic Emotional State as Song Inspiration
podcast.body: The lyrics and theme of "Love Will Tear Us Apart" are directly rooted in Ian Curtis's tragic emotional situation. He found himself caught between two women, his wife and his lover, neither of whom he truly wanted, and both of whom caused him significant distress. "la historia va de la tránsica situación sintial que tenía y en curtes y enfrascada entre dos mujeres a las que no quería y que la cien al bien posible, que era su mujer y su avante."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Love will Tear us appart. Una historia increible.

podcast.title: Unavailability and Others Singing at Concerts
podcast.body: During the band's final months, Ian Curtis's health problems sometimes led to his unavailability to sing at concerts, resulting in other Joy Division members taking over vocal duties. "tenemos incluso trozos ya cantados por otros miembros de joy de visión ante la disponibilidad que tenía y Ian Cortes para cantar a veces."

podcast.title: Voice Transformation for 'Closer'
podcast.body: During the recording of the "Closer" album in March 1980, producer Martin Hannett and Factory Records head Tony Wilson coached Ian to achieve a deeper and richer vocal delivery by having him listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records, which resulted in a more haunting and authoritative sound that made his portrayals of pain and alienation highly credible. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."

xref.title: Ian Curtis's Epilepsy Diagnosis (January 23, 1979)
xref.body: Ian Curtis began experiencing seizures in the fall of 1978, which rapidly became frequent. On January 23, 1979, his diagnosis of epilepsy was confirmed, described as a grim and severe case, with a doctor warning that his life would be dominated by the disease unless he adhered to a regimen of strong medication. "Ian started having seizures in the fall of 1978. They quickly became frequent. On January 23rd, 1979, the diagnosis was confirmed. And the diagnosis was grim. His case was really bad."

xref.title: Depression and Personal Turmoil (April 1980)
xref.body: By April 1980, Ian Curtis was severely depressed, a state compounded not only by his epilepsy but also by a failing affair with a Belgian fan, the impending split from his wife, and dire financial difficulties that forced them to give away their family dog. He desired solitude but was ill-equipped to live alone. "By April 1980, Ian was very, very depressed. Not just as a result of the epilepsy either. He was having an affair with a Belgian fan. That wasn't going well. He and his wife were on the verge of splitting up. Money was so tight that they had to give away the family dog. He wanted to be alone but really wasn't equipped to live alone."

xref.title: Final Concert and Seizure (May 2, 1980)
xref.body: Joy Division's last concert was held at Birmingham University on May 2, 1980, and was recorded. During the performance of "Decades," Ian Curtis fainted on stage due to an epileptic seizure. The audience initially mistook his collapse for an intense dance move and cheered. Curtis was helped off stage, recovered, and returned for an encore, marking his final stage appearance. He died by suicide less than two weeks later. "The final joy division gig was held on May 2nd, 1980 at Birmingham University. The show was recorded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Legendary Gigs

xref.title: Ian Curtis's Struggles (Spring 1980)
xref.body: By spring 1980, Ian Curtis was battling drugs and alcohol, having an affair, and contemplating divorcing his wife. He suffered from severe epilepsy, with seizures becoming more frequent and medication having little effect. Despite the band's rising success and a booked American tour, Curtis was terribly depressed and considering quitting the band to open a bookshop on the continent. "Singer Ian Curtis was battling drugs in alcohol. He was having an affair with a Belgian woman while his wife went to work and cared for their baby daughter. And Ian had a severe case of epilepsy which seemed to be getting worse and worse."

xref.title: Ian Curtis's Suicide (1980)
xref.body: Ian Curtis's death by suicide cut short Joy Division's potential, but it ultimately cemented their legend. His untimely passing contributed to the band's status as one of the most influential British indie bands of the 20th century and beyond. "His death, though, spawned a legend, and Joy Division has become one of the great influential British indie bands of the 20th century."

xref.title: Suicide (May 18, 1980)
xref.body: After previous suicide attempts, Ian Curtis took his own life by hanging himself from a clothesline in his kitchen in the early morning hours of May 18, 1980. This tragic event occurred on the very day Joy Division was scheduled to depart for their first-ever tour of North America. "There had been some suicide attempts. By the early morning hours of May 18, 1980, Ian couldn't take it anymore. He hanged himself from the clothesline in the kitchen of his house. That Monday was the day joy division was supposed to leave for their first ever tour of North America."

xref.title: Band Pact and Dissolution
xref.body: The other three members were devastated by Ian Curtis's death and had made a pact that if any member left for any reason, the band would automatically self-destruct. This meant Joy Division was officially over, but the surviving members chose to create something new together. "And they had all made a pact. Should any member leave for any reason, the band would automatically self-destruct."

xref.title: Band's Rising Fortunes Amidst Singer's Struggles
xref.body: By spring 1980, Joy Division's career was on an upward trajectory with two critically acclaimed albums and a booked American tour. Simultaneously, singer Ian Curtis was battling severe personal issues, including drug and alcohol abuse, an affair, worsening epilepsy, and profound depression, leading him to consider quitting the band and divorcing his wife. "Meanwhile, Joy Division's fortunes as a band were looking up. The first album had been a critical success and there were indications that the just-release second album was also going to do well. A tour of America had been booked and expectations were high, very high."

xref.title: Battle of the Bands and Tony Wilson
xref.body: On April 14, 1978, Joy Division competed in a Battle of the Bands at Rafters, hoping to secure a record deal. Ian Curtis, believing Tony Wilson (host of the TV show "So It Goes") needed to know about the band, approached him with an "angry, insulting letter" rather than polite conversation, which unexpectedly impressed Wilson enough to book Joy Division on his show. "Ian believed that Tony definitely needed to know about Joy Division. But instead of being all polite and respectful, Ian just slammed the guy, complete with a very angry, very insulting letter."

xref.title: Death Date Coincidence – 37 Years After Ian Curtis, Close to Chester Bennington
xref.body: Cornell died by hanging on May 18, 2017 — exactly 37 years to the day that Joy Division singer Ian Curtis hanged himself. Two months later, on July 20, 2017 (which would have been Cornell's 53rd birthday), his close friend Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died by suicide, also by hanging. Cornell is interred at Hollywood Forever Cemetery in Los Angeles; his tombstone reads "Voice of our generation and an artist for all time." Johnny Ramone's monument is nearby. "Two months after Chris died, July 20, 2017, which would have been Chris' 53rd birthday, his close friend Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died by suicide."

srcs.episode: 10 Things About Chris Cornell

xref.title: Early Awareness of Father's Music
xref.body: Natalie Curtis was 13 months old when her father, Ian Curtis, died. She first learned he was a singer when she was about three years old, told by her mother. As she grew up, she was mostly an "outside observer" to the Joy Division phenomenon but gradually became aware that her dad was the subject of much discussion. "She would have been 13 months old when dad died. What became of her? Well she first learned that dad was a singer when she was about three, mom told her."

xref.body: The band's initial name was "the stiff kittens," which Ian Curtis disliked because he felt it made them sound like generic punk bands. "At first, they were called the stiff kittens, but Ian hated that name because he felt it made them sound like any other punk band."

xref.title: Epilepsy Diagnosis and Medication Struggle
xref.body: Ian Curtis began experiencing seizures in late 1978, with an official diagnosis of severe epilepsy confirmed on January 23, 1979. He was prescribed a heavy medication regimen, but many of the drugs were ineffective or caused severe side effects, including extreme mood swings, and his condition worsened due to late nights, touring pressures, heavy smoking, and large amounts of alcohol. "The official diagnosis came on January 23rd, 1979. Here's classified his case as severe and a heavy regime of medication was prescribed." "Many of the drugs did not work or only work for a short period of time."

xref.title: Family Royalty Stream
xref.body: Thanks to the band's posthumous success, Ian Curtis's widow, Deborah, and his daughter now receive a "nice stream of royalty checks," indicating a significant improvement in their financial well-being. "The good news in all this is that Ian's widow, Deborah, and his daughter now receive a nice stream of royalty checks."

xref.title: Final Days and Suicide
xref.body: In his final days, Ian Curtis, isolated and mentally/physically unwell, watched the Werner Herzog film "Strozek," about a struggling musician, drank strong coffee and whiskey, and wrote a long note to his estranged wife Deborah, with pictures of his wife and baby daughter nearby. On Sunday, May 18, 1980, at approximately 11 AM, Deborah returned home and found Ian had hung himself in the kitchen using an old-fashioned clothes rack. "Once Deborah was gone, Ian sat down to watch a movie on the telly. A 1977 Werner Herzog film entitled Strozek." "And within seconds, she ran into the street, screaming. Ian had hung himself in the kitchen using an old-fashioned clothes rack that could be raised and lowered from the ceiling using a rope and pulley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

xref.title: Final Gig as Warsaw
xref.body: The band performed their last gig under the name Warsaw on New Year's Eve, 1977, before officially adopting "Joy Division." "So after one last gig as Warsaw on New Year's Eve 1977, Ian Curtis, Barney Albrecht, soon to become Bernie Sumner, Peter Hook and Steven Morris became Joy Division officially."

xref.title: Formation After Joy Division
xref.body: Following the death of Ian Curtis and the honoring of Joy Division's "suicide pact," Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word to dissolve Joy Division and immediately began working on their next project, which eventually became New Order. "So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word. Joy Division was retired, and work was started on the next project, which would eventually be known as New Order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Formation and Influential Sound
xref.body: New Order formed from the surviving members of Joy Division following Ian Curtis's suicide in 1980. Their subsequent career proved as influential as their first, successfully bridging dance music with post-punk indie culture. Their Joy Division legacy provided unquestionable coolness and indie credentials. "When singer Ian Curtis committed suicide in 1980, the rest of the band regrouped as new order. That second act in their career turned out to be just as influential as their first."

srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: After Ian Curtis's death, surviving Joy Division members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, and Stephen Morris discussed their future. Encouraged by their progress as Joy Division, they decided to move forward under a new name. Their manager, Rob Gretton, suggested "New Order" after finding the phrase in a newspaper headline about mass killings in Pol Pot's Cambodia. "Their manager, my name Rob Greten, is the one who came up with it. He found the name in a newspaper headline about the mass killings in Pol Potts, Cambodia. The phrase was new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Formation from Joy Division
xref.body: Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980, Joy Division was reborn as New Order, with Rob Gretton continuing as their manager. Gretton's involvement went beyond typical management, as he assisted the band with tasks like sorting song titles and even sang backup on some of their recordings.

xref.title: Formation from Joy Division's Ashes
xref.body: New Order was formed from the remaining members of Joy Division after Ian Curtis's death. The band became "Uber Influential," which in turn led a considerable number of new fans to discover and purchase Joy Division's earlier records. "New order, the band that formed out of the ashes of Joy Division, also became Uber Influential, which led a lot of new people to buy Joy Division records."

xref.title: Funding the First Record
xref.body: To finance the recording and pressing of 1200 copies of their first record, Ian Curtis deceitfully told his bank manager he needed 400 pounds for "dining room furniture," with the money instead going directly to the band's musical endeavor, ready by July 1978. "He told his bank manager that he needed 400 pounds to buy some dining room furniture. But when the money came through, it went straight towards the recording and pressing of 1200 copies of the first Jordy Vision record."

xref.title: Ian Curtis's Dance Style
xref.body: Ian Curtis was known for his "unique, herky, jerky way of dancing on stage." This distinctive style led the audience at Joy Division's final concert to initially mistake his epileptic seizure for an energetic performance collapse. "The audience thought it was all part of the act because Ian had this unique, herky, jerky way of dancing on stage and many people in the audience just looked like he had collapsed from dancing so hard."

xref.title: Ian Curtis's Personal Turmoil
xref.body: The lyrics for "Love Will Tear Us Apart" were deeply personal, drawn from the considerable turmoil in Ian Curtis's life. This included his epilepsy, which was growing worse due to drugs, alcohol, late nights, smoking bad food, and the stress of holding down a day job while being in a struggling band. His failing marriage to Deborah and an affair with a Belgian woman named Anaconda Rae also contributed significantly to his emotional state reflected in the song. "Curtis's lyrics were drawn from the turmoil in his life."

xref.title: Ian's Desire to Leave the Band
xref.body: Following a period of intense illness and depression, Ian Curtis announced his intention to leave Joy Division, expressing a desire to move to Holland and open a bookshop, although he retracted this statement just a day later as if he had never said it. "Then he announced he was leaving the band. He was going to move to Holland to open a bookshop."

xref.title: Ian's Fear of Hurting Daughter
xref.body: Following the birth of his daughter, Natalie, Ian Curtis loved his baby but was afraid to pick her up or even touch her due to the intensifying frequency and severity of his epileptic seizures, fearing he might inadvertently harm her during an attack. "He loved his baby, but he was afraid to pick her up or even touch her for fear that he would have a seizure and hurt her."

xref.title: Increased Darkness Post-Suicide
xref.body: The band was already known for its dark sound, but the suicide of lead singer Ian Curtis intensified this perception, adding to the "doomed" mystique of the group and fueling the burgeoning Goth scene. "Now they were dark already, but when their doomed lead singer killed himself, that just added fuel to the fire."

xref.title: Influence on Ian Curtis
xref.body: Ian Curtis's interest in music significantly escalated after he attended a Sex Pistols concert at the Manchester Free Trade Hall on July 20, 1976, where he was one of only a few dozen people in the audience and easily spotted wearing a jacket with the word "hate" on the back. "His interest in music really took off when he was one of a few dozen people in the audience, when the sex pistols played the Manchester Free Hall on July 20th, 1976."

xref.body: The band that would become Joy Division initially went by the name "Warsaw" after Ian Curtis rejected "Stiff Kittens." This name was inspired by David Bowie's song "Warzawe" from his "Low" album. "Everyone soon settled on Warsaw. That sounded different."

xref.title: Initial Openness and Later Withdrawal on Epilepsy
xref.body: Initially, Ian Curtis was very proactive about his epilepsy, joining the British Epilepsy Association and openly discussing his condition. However, he soon ceased being open, eventually refusing to talk about it altogether. "At first, Ian was very proactive, joining the British Epilepsy Association and was willing to talk to anybody about what he faced. But he soon stopped being so open about his condition and eventually refused to talk about it."

xref.title: Legacy and Influence
xref.body: Joy Division was a foundational band for Factory Records. Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in 1980, the remaining members regrouped to form New Order. Their "Joy Division heritage" provided New Order with "unassailable, unquestionable" coolness and indie credentials, ensuring their continued influence. "Factory had been the label of Joy Division. When singer Ian Curtis committed suicide in 1980, the rest of the band regrouped as new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

xref.title: Lyrics Reflecting Relationships
xref.body: Specific lines in "Love Will Tear Us Apart," such as "why is the bedroom so cold and turned away on your side," are understood to be direct expressions from Ian Curtis, speaking to either his wife Deborah or his girlfriend Anaconda Rae, or both. This reveals the deeply personal and autobiographical nature of the song's emotional core. "Lines like why is the bedroom so cold and turned away on your side aren't just lines plucked from somewhere, he's speaking to one or both women in his life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stories Behind Songs - 5

xref.title: Martin Hannett's Production Obsession
xref.body: During the recording sessions for "Love Will Tear Us Apart," producer Martin Hannett became intensely obsessed with the song. He meticulously recorded each instrument separately and spent a significant amount of time perfecting Ian Curtis's voice in the mix. His dedication was so extreme that he once called drummer Steven Morris at 4 AM, demanding he come to the studio immediately because he couldn't get the snare drum sound right, and frequently called the band in the middle of the night to hear the latest mix. "Hannet mixed and remix the song again and again and again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stories Behind Songs - 5

xref.title: Medication Side Effects and Personal Impact
xref.body: The medication Ian Curtis was taking for his epilepsy caused wild mood swings. The fear of having a seizure while holding his baby daughter made him hesitant to embrace her, and he was known to suffer at least two severe seizures weekly. "The men, he was on, caused wild mood swings. When his wife gave birth to a baby daughter, Ian was afraid to hold her or less the seizure begin and he actually hurt her. He could be counted on to have at least two giant seizures a week."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

xref.title: Mini Riot at Derby Hall
xref.body: On April 8, 1980, after Ian Curtis's overdose attempt, the band played at Derby Hall, where a shaky Ian was only able to sing two songs. The crowd reacted so negatively that a mini-riot ensued, resulting in five people being hospitalized. "Ian was so shaky that he was only able to sing two songs, and the crowd freaked out. Five people ended up being taken to the hospital after a mini riot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Missed American Tour and Triumph
xref.body: Ian Curtis committed suicide just hours before Joy Division was scheduled to embark on their very first American tour. This tragic event occurred on the eve of what was perceived as a potential "gigantic, artistic, and commercial triumph" for the group. "Ian Curtis hung himself literally just hours before Joy Division was supposed to leave on their very first American tour."

xref.title: NME Cover and Fan Influence
xref.body: Ian Curtis's appearance on the cover of NME in January 1979, wearing a dark raincoat, inspired die-hard fans to begin attending Joy Division gigs dressed in the same manner, highlighting the band's burgeoning visual impact and cult following. "When Ian appeared on the cover of the enemy in January 1979 wearing a dark raincoat, die-hard fans started attending gigs dressed the same way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Name "Warsaw" Inspiration
xref.body: After rejecting "Stiff Kittens," the band settled on "Warsaw," inspired by the song "Warzawe" from David Bowie's "Low" album, reflecting Ian Curtis's admiration for Bowie. "Besides, they were inspired by a song called Warzawe on David Bowie's low album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Name Choice as Counterpoint
xref.body: Almost a decade after Ian Curtis's death, another Manchester band, the Happy Mondays, deliberately chose their name to "counteract all that gloom," providing a stylistic and thematic contrast to the dark aesthetic of Joy Division. "And almost a decade later, another Manchester bad tried to counteract all that gloom by naming themselves the Happy Mondays."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: On-Stage Seizures and Collapse
xref.body: Ian Curtis's epilepsy frequently affected his live performances. During one studio session, he fell, hit his head on a sink, and lay unconscious. Strobe lights at a show once induced a seizure, requiring him to be carried off stage, an event that was not isolated, as he collapsed regularly during gigs. "One night in the studio, he fell and hit his head on the sink and laid unconscious on the floor. During a show that featured strobe lights, a seizure was induced and he had to be carried off stage. And that wasn't the first time. Ian collapsed during gigs almost regularly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

xref.title: Origin of "Joy Division" Name
xref.body: The name "Joy Division" was chosen by Ian Curtis, inspired by a passage in Carol Satinsky's 1971 book "House of Dolls," which described "Joy Division" as a section in a concentration camp where women were forced to perform sexual favors for Nazi officers on leave, reflecting Ian's fascination with Nazi Germany. "The Joy Division was where women were forced to do sexual favors for Nazi officers on leave. I mean, how dark is that?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Other Health Issues
xref.body: Besides epilepsy and profound depression, Ian Curtis also suffered from an allergy to sunlight, which caused his hands to become red and swollen. "He had many health problems. Depression was one. He developed an allergy to sunlight which caused his hands to go red and swell up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

xref.title: Performance-Related Seizures
xref.body: Ian Curtis experienced grand mal seizures during at least two performances, one triggered by strobe lights and another so violent that audience members feared for his life. His condition deteriorated to the point where even percussion effects could induce an epileptic episode, leading to a minder being assigned to ensure he took his medication, avoided alcohol, and got sufficient sleep. "There were at least two occasions when he had a grand mal seizure in the middle of a performance. One triggered by strobe lights and another that was so violent, people were genuinely afraid that he was going to die."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

xref.title: Personal Turmoil and Suicide Attempt
xref.body: Ian Curtis faced significant personal challenges, including a difficult relationship with his wife Deborah, who had initiated divorce proceedings, and an affair with a Belgian fan, Enneke van Array. On April 6, 1980, he made a suicide attempt by overdosing on pills, requiring an ambulance and a stomach pump, yet a doctor inexplicably deemed him not suicidal and sent him home, after which he was so shaky at a gig that he could only perform two songs. "There was a suicide attempt on Sunday, April 6, 1980 when Ian died a bunch of pills." "He told his mates that he had a terrible claustrophobic feeling like he was caught in a whirlpool of being sucked down and drowning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

xref.title: Post-Mortem Influence and Sales Surge
xref.body: After the death of Ian Curtis, Joy Division's fortunes significantly improved. The band became recognized as one of the most influential post-punk bands of all time, and their records continue to sell in large quantities through multiple generations of music fans. The subsequent formation of New Order also contributed to increased sales of Joy Division's records by introducing the music to new audiences. "Joy Division's fortunes took off. They are considered to be one of the most influential post-punk bands of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

xref.title: Post-Mortem Legacy and Influence
xref.body: Since Ian Curtis's death in May 1980, Joy Division has achieved legendary status, with continued album sales, radio play, streams, and hundreds of bootlegs in circulation. Their sound and style profoundly influenced the development of Goth, industrial music, Emo, and the alternative music scene of the 80s and 90s (through New Order), demonstrating how rock could be emotionally powerful, stripped down, intellectually serious, and a study in mental illness and emotional paralysis. "Since that day in May 1980, joy division has become legendary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Posthumous Headstone and Theft
xref.body: Ian Curtis's body was cremated after his funeral on May 23rd, and a headstone was placed in Macklesfield Cemetery bearing the inscription "Ian Curtis, 18580, Love Will Terrace Apart." This headstone was stolen in 2008 but was eventually replaced. "That headstone was stolen in 2008, but it was eventually replaced."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

xref.title: Predecessor to New Order
xref.body: Joy Division was the band that preceded New Order, sharing members before the death of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980. New Order initially retained Joy Division's dark, guitar-driven musical style. "Now, at first, New Order sounded a lot like Joy Division, which is to say they played dark guitar-driven stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 4: Alt-Dance

xref.title: Proposed Museum at Barton Street
xref.body: There has been a persistent interest in transforming the house at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, where Ian Curtis lived and died, into a Joy Division museum, reflecting the ongoing fascination with the band and its frontman. "And the last I heard, some people still want to turn the house at 77 Barton Street in Mackelsfield into a Joy Division museum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Rebirth from Joy Division
xref.body: Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980, Joy Division was reborn as New Order, with Rob Gretton continuing as their manager. Gretton's involvement went beyond typical management, as he assisted the band with tasks like sorting song titles and even sang backup on some of their recordings.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock

xref.title: Shared London Gig
xref.body: Joy Division performed a show with The Stranglers at a London venue called the Rainbow on April 4, 1980, during which Ian Curtis suffered three attacks in the first five songs and later collapsed entirely. "On April 4, 1980, during a show with the stranglers at a London venue called the Rainbow, Ian suffered three attacks during the first five songs of the set before collapsing entirely."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Singer's Health and Performance
xref.body: Lead singer Ian Curtis's jerky dancing style was attributed to his suffering from drug abuse and epilepsy, leading to paranoid and desperate lyrics that perfectly matched the band's minimalist music. "In the old days, the village shaman would have said that singer Ian Curtis was possessed, judging by his jerky ways of dancing. And in fact, he was possessed. He was suffering from the twin demons of drug abuse and epilepsy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

xref.title: Suicide Pact and Band Dissolution
xref.body: A solemn suicide pact existed among the members of Joy Division, stipulating that if any member were to leave the band for any reason, Joy Division would cease to exist. Consequently, upon Ian Curtis's death, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris honored their word, retiring Joy Division and beginning work on their next project, New Order. "The deal was that should any member leave for any reason joy division would be broken up. So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Tony Wilson's Vocal Suggestion
xref.body: Tony Wilson of Factory Records suggested to Ian Curtis that he try using his baritone range when singing "Love Will Tear Us Apart," in a manner similar to Frank Sinatra. Curtis adopted this suggestion, adding a "very old-school crooning" element to his vocal performance on the track. "Tony Wilson of the band's factory records made a suggestion. Ian tried using the baritone range in the same way Frank Sinatra would when you sing this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stories Behind Songs - 5

xref.title: Uncategorizable Sound and Style
xref.body: Joy Division, an archetypical British indie band from Manchester, developed a unique "strange spooky paranoid sound" in the late 70s. Their music was minimalist with Ian Curtis's distinct vocals, and live performances featured his "weird, strange, jerky" dance moves, influencing fans to adopt a dark 3-quarter length raincoat as an unofficial uniform. They defied easy categorization, being too dour for New Wave and not thrashing enough for punk, highlighting their distinctiveness within the post-punk movement. "By the late 70s, Joy Division had developed a strange spooky paranoid sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

xref.title: Vocal Coaching Influence
xref.body: During the recording of Joy Division's "Closer" album, Ian Curtis was made to listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records by producer Martin Hannett and Tony Wilson. This unusual coaching technique was aimed at helping Ian develop a deeper, richer, and more authoritative vocal delivery, which contributed to the album's haunting sound. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Worsening Condition and Lifestyle Factors
xref.body: Despite trying various anti-convulsant drugs, Ian Curtis's epilepsy showed little improvement. His lifestyle, including touring, late nights, drinking, smoking, and drug use, was detrimental, leading to increasingly frequent and stronger seizures throughout 1979 and early 1980. "Meanwhile, many different anti-convulsants were tried with little effect. Turing, the late nights, the drinking, the smoking, and the drugs did not help. And the seizures became more frequent and stronger through 1979 and early 1980."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
